title: The Day of the Dead
hookLine: in Mexico, All Souls is kept with altars, marigolds and photographs

lines: A PHOTOGRAPH IN A PRESSED SHIRT.
MARIGOLDS IN A PATH TO THE DOOR.
STAYING A WHILE AT THE GRAVE.
cards: A table against the living room wall, covered in a bright cloth. On it, a framed photograph of a grandfather in a pressed shirt.
Beside him, a glass of water, a candle, a plate of sweet bread, a pack of the cigarettes he never quit, and a bottle of the soda he liked. Marigolds everywhere, petals in a path to the door.
A crucifix or Our Lady of Guadalupe watches over it all. Later, the family will clean his grave, bring flowers, and stay a while.

teach.b: First, the calendar. The Church keeps the Solemnity of All Saints and, the next day, the Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed, All Souls, which you met in year two, when Catholics pray for everyone who has died.

In Mexico, those two days became the Día de Muertos, the Day of the Dead, kept at home altars and in cemeteries as well as at Mass. Historians discuss how much it also carries older Indigenous ways of honoring the dead.
Second, the altar, the ofrenda, which means an offering. Photographs, so faces aren't forgotten. Favorite food and drink, because love remembers details.
Candles, for light. Marigolds, whose color and scent, people say, help the dead find their way home. Those meanings are tradition, held with affection.
Third, why a Catholic can keep it with joy.
The book of Wisdom, in the Douay-Rheims: "But the souls of the just are in the hand of God, and the torment of death shall not touch them."
Catholics believe the dead are alive in God, and that the living can still pray for them. So it isn't spooky, or a version of Halloween.
It's a family reunion across the line of death, with the Church's prayers at its center.

teach.h: A WEEK OF FAITH AT HOME.
teach.b: Last, this week faith kept leaving the sanctuary: a Mass for someone, a fast, alms in Lent, a Jesse tree, walking wise men, an Easter basket.

teach.h: THE SOULS OF THE JUST ARE IN THE HAND OF GOD.
teach.b: Today the whole family joins it at home, the living and the dead.

how: In Mexico and among Mexican families elsewhere, Catholics keep All Saints and All Souls as the Día de Muertos: they build home altars with photographs, candles, marigolds and the favorite foods of those who have died, visit and decorate graves, and pray for the dead, often including Mass.

practice: Choose one person who has died; if you have a picture nearby, look at their face. Remember one small thing they loved, a food, a song, a joke, a chair they always sat in, and let a smile come if it comes.

If you pray, ask God to give them eternal rest; if you don't, say their name and thank them for one thing. If grief feels too heavy to carry alone, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: The Day of the Dead. Día de Muertos: Mexico's way of keeping All Saints and All Souls, with home altars, marigolds, photographs and visits to the graves. Today's word.

orig.note: Spanish, the Day of the Dead: the name used in Mexico for the days of All Saints and All Souls.
